parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Nayland Water**
> 
> Nayland Water designs and installs water treatment systems in country E. It is appraising a new plant costing \$2.4 million with an expected life of ten years.
> 
> The appraisal produces:
> 
> - a net present value of \$410 000 at a discount rate of 8%
> - a payback period of 6 years 2 months
> 
> The forecast assumes revenue grows 5% a year for ten years. Nayland's revenue has grown at 5% a year for the last three years.
> 
> Two of Nayland's four largest contracts are with the government and are re-tendered every three years.
> 
> Nayland's bank has indicated that borrowing costs will rise. At a discount rate of 11%, the net present value becomes negative.
> 
> The treatment technology used in the plant is expected to be superseded within about eight years.

Evaluate whether Nayland Water can rely on its investment appraisal when deciding to proceed with the new plant.
parts.solution_md:
Investment appraisal produces figures from forecasts, so its usefulness depends on how sound those forecasts are **[K]**. Nayland's net present value of \$410 000 rests on revenue growing 5% a year for ten years **[Ap]**. That rate matches the last three years, so it is not invented, but two of the four largest contracts are with the government and are re-tendered every three years, meaning roughly half the revenue base is re-competed three times during the project's life **[An]**. A single lost tender would break the growth assumption early, and because net present value compounds those flows across ten years the error would widen rather than stay contained **[An]**

The discount rate is a second weakness **[K]**. The appraisal uses 8%, but the bank has indicated borrowing costs will rise, and at 11% the net present value becomes negative **[Ap]**. The project therefore sits close to the boundary between adding and destroying value, and what decides which side it falls on is a rate Nayland does not control **[An]**. A net present value of \$410 000 on a \$2.4 million investment is a thin margin for a ten-year commitment, and it disappears on a three-point movement in a single input **[An]**

Nayland cannot rely on this appraisal as it stands **[E]**. That is not because the arithmetic is wrong; the methods have been applied properly and give a genuine result at the assumptions used **[E]**. The problem is that both key assumptions are fragile in the same direction, and a payback of 6 years 2 months on technology expected to be superseded within about eight leaves almost no margin if either moves **[E]**. Appraisal is most dependable over short horizons and least dependable exactly where Nayland is using it, a decade ahead in a market where the technology and half the customer base both turn over **[E]**. Nayland should test the net present value across a range of discount rates and growth assumptions rather than presenting one figure, and should not commit until it knows whether the project survives the loss of a government contract **[E]**. If it does not, the appraisal will have told the directors something considerably more useful than the \$410 000 did **[E]**

However, the technology estimate is itself uncertain, and treatment plant often remains serviceable well beyond the point at which newer equipment appears
> - Nayland could test the net present value across a range of discount rates and growth assumptions rather than presenting a single figure. However, sensitivity analysis takes time and expertise, and a range of outcomes can make a decision harder to take rather than easier
> - Nayland could delay until it knows whether the government contracts renew. However, delay may mean losing the opportunity, and the contracts are re-tendered repeatedly, so there is no point at which that uncertainty disappears
>

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Radlett Timber**
> 
> Radlett Timber runs a sawmill in country S, employing 60 people. It is the largest employer in its town. Its customers are furniture makers who buy from Radlett because it supplies hand-finished, made-to-order timber.
> 
> Radlett is choosing between two investments:
> 
> - **Option 1: an automated cutting line.** Net present value \$620 000. It would replace 22 of the 60 workers and produces standard sizes only.
> - **Option 2: upgrading the existing line.** Net present value \$310 000. No redundancies.
> 
> Radlett's directors promised employees in 2025 that there would be no compulsory redundancies before 2028.
> 
> The automated line's net present value assumes the mill runs at 85% capacity. Over the last three years Radlett has averaged 68%.

Evaluate whether Radlett Timber should choose the automated cutting line rather than upgrading its existing line.
parts.solution_md:
Net present value measures the value a project adds once future cash flows are discounted to today's terms **[K]**. The automated line has a net present value of \$620 000 against \$310 000 for the upgrade, exactly double **[Ap]**. On quantitative grounds the decision looks settled, since the same method and the same discount rate show one option adding twice the value of the other **[An]**. Rejecting it would mean giving up \$310 000 of forecast value, which the directors would have to justify to shareholders **[An]**

The qualitative factors point the other way **[K]**. The automated line would replace 22 of 60 workers in the town's largest employer, and the directors promised no compulsory redundancies before 2028 **[Ap]**. Breaking that promise would damage trust among the 38 who remain, and in a small town where the mill is the main employer the effect reaches customers and the local authority too **[An]**. Radlett would also lose the hand-finished, made-to-order work its furniture makers buy it for, since the automated line produces standard sizes only, so the higher figure is being earned by abandoning the business's point of difference **[An]**

Radlett should not choose the automated line on these figures **[E]**. The gap between the two is large, and were it reliable the qualitative arguments alone might not be enough to overturn it **[E]**. What weakens it is that the \$620 000 assumes 85% capacity while the mill has averaged 68% over three years, so at anything close to its actual utilisation the advantage narrows sharply or disappears **[E]**. That is the more serious objection, because it means the quantitative case is not as strong as it looks rather than merely being outweighed by other considerations **[E]**. Radlett should recalculate the automated line at 68% and across a range of realistic utilisations before comparing the two, and should proceed with the upgrade unless the automated line remains clearly ahead under assumptions the mill has actually achieved **[E]**

> | **3** | - Shows understanding of one factor affecting the investment decision in context |
> | **2** | - Shows knowledge of two factors affecting the investment decision |
> | **1** | - Shows knowledge of one factor affecting the investment decision |
> 
> **Analysis and evaluation**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **5** | - An evaluative statement or recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **4** | - Argument based on two factors affecting the investment decision in context |
> | **3** | - Argument based on one factor affecting the investment decision in context |
> | **2** | - Analysis of two factors affecting the investment decision |
> | **1** | - Analysis of one factor affecting the investment decision |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Radlett could choose the automated line. Its net present value of \$620 000 is double the upgrade's \$310 000, both are appraised on the same basis so the comparison is valid on its own terms, and automation may reduce unit costs and improve consistency. However, the \$620 000 assumes 85% capacity while the mill has averaged 68% over three years, so the figure is not dependable
> - Rejecting \$310 000 of forecast added value requires justification to the owners, and a business that declines the better-performing option needs a clear reason. However, recalculating at realistic utilisation may remove the advantage altogether, in which case there is nothing to justify
> - The automated line would replace 22 of 60 workers in the town's largest employer and break a promise of no compulsory redundancies before 2028, damaging trust among the 38 who remain. However, refusing all automation indefinitely may put more jobs at risk later if competitors mechanise and Radlett cannot match their costs
> - Standard sizes only would end the hand-finished, made-to-order work customers buy Radlett for, so the higher return is earned by abandoning its point of difference. However, some customers may value lower prices more than bespoke sizing, which the case does not establish either way
> - Radlett could choose the upgrade, which protects the competitive position while still adding \$310 000 of value and requiring no redundancies. However, it forgoes whatever genuine efficiency automation would bring, and the mill's equipment still needs to remain competitive
> - Radlett could revisit automation later if utilisation genuinely rises towards 85%. However, delay may mean the technology or the supplier terms have changed, and competitors may have moved first
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> **Torrin**
> 
> Torrin hires out excavators and diggers to builders in country N. It is choosing between two machines, each costing \$240 000.
> 
> **Table 1.1 Forecast net cash inflows (\$)**
> 
> |   | Machine A | Machine B |
> |---|---|---|
> | Year 1 | 110 000 | 40 000 |
> | Year 2 | 100 000 | 60 000 |
> | Year 3 | 40 000 | 90 000 |
> | Year 4 | 20 000 | 120 000 |
> | Year 5 | 10 000 | 140 000 |
> 
> Torrin's finance director appraises every project using payback alone, and applies a rule that an investment must pay back within three years. Machine A pays back in 2 years 9 months and Machine B in 3 years 5 months.
> 
> Torrin has an overdraft of \$90 000 which its bank has asked it to reduce. Machine B is a newer model with lower emissions, and country N introduces emissions rules for hire equipment in 2029.
> 
> Torrin's owner says the business has always used payback and it has never let them down.

Evaluate whether Torrin should continue to rely on the payback method when choosing between the two machines.
parts.solution_md:
Payback measures how long an investment takes to recover its initial cost **[K]**. Machine A pays back in 2 years 9 months and Machine B in 3 years 5 months, so under Torrin's three-year rule only A qualifies **[Ap]**. That rule is not arbitrary: Torrin has a \$90 000 overdraft the bank wants reduced, and a machine returning its cost nine months sooner frees cash to do exactly that **[An]**. For a business under pressure from its lender, knowing when the money comes back may genuinely matter more than knowing how much eventually arrives **[An]**

The difficulty is what payback ignores **[K]**. Machine A generates \$280 000 across five years while Machine B generates \$450 000, a difference of \$170 000 **[Ap]**. Payback stops counting the moment the initial cost is recovered, so every dollar Machine B earns in years four and five is invisible to the decision, even though those are the years in which it earns most **[An]**. Choosing A means rejecting \$170 000 of cash inflow because it arrives eight months later than a rule of thumb permits **[An]**

Torrin should not rely on payback alone **[E]**. The method suits its immediate position, and with the bank pressing on the overdraft it would be wrong to treat liquidity as a secondary concern **[E]**. But payback answers a narrower question than the one Torrin faces, because a three-year cut-off measures speed rather than value, and here eight months is being allowed to outweigh \$170 000 **[E]**. The 2029 emissions rules strengthen the point further, since Machine A's later cash flows may not be achievable at all if an older machine cannot legally be hired out **[E]**. Torrin should calculate net present value for both machines and treat payback as a constraint rather than the decision itself, perhaps discussing a short extension of the overdraft with the bank on the strength of Machine B's forecast returns **[E]**

> | **3** | - Shows understanding of one investment appraisal method in context |
> | **2** | - Shows knowledge of two investment appraisal methods |
> | **1** | - Shows knowledge of one investment appraisal method |
> 
> **Analysis and evaluation**
> 
> | **Mark** | **Descriptor** |
> |---|---|
> | **8** | - Justified recommendation with developed weighing of key arguments in business context |
> | **7** | - Justified recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **6** | - Developed recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **5** | - An evaluative statement or recommendation based on arguments in context |
> | **4** | - Argument based on two investment appraisal methods in context |
> | **3** | - Argument based on one investment appraisal method in context |
> | **2** | - Analysis of two investment appraisal methods |
> | **1** | - Analysis of one investment appraisal method |
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Torrin could continue to rely on payback and choose Machine A. It pays back nine months sooner, releasing cash to reduce the \$90 000 overdraft the bank has asked it to cut, and payback is quick to apply and easily understood in an owner-managed business. However, Machine B generates \$450 000 against Machine A's \$280 000, so the rule rejects \$170 000 of inflow over an eight-month difference
> - Payback reduces risk by favouring projects with shorter exposure, which matters where equipment values and demand are uncertain. However, it ignores every cash flow after the recovery point, and years four and five are exactly when Machine B earns most
> - The three-year cut-off gives a clear and consistent decision rule that removes argument. However, it is a rule of thumb rather than a measure of value added, and it ignores the time value of money entirely, unlike net present value
> - The 2029 emissions rules may make Machine A's later inflows unachievable if an older machine cannot legally be hired out, which payback would never have counted anyway. However, those rules are three years away and their detail is not yet known, so the risk is real but not quantifiable
> - Torrin could calculate net present value for both machines and use payback as a constraint rather than the decision. However, that requires a discount rate the business may not be able to justify, and it takes time a small firm may not have
> - The overdraft problem may be solvable by negotiation, whereas \$170 000 of forgone inflow is not recoverable. However, a bank already pressing for reduction may refuse an extension, in which case the liquidity constraint is real rather than negotiable
> 
> Accept any other valid response

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** reason why a business might use more than one investment appraisal method.
parts.solution_md:
Each method measures something different: payback measures speed of recovery, the accounting rate of return measures profitability, and net present value measures value added after discounting **[1]**. A business uses several because a project can look attractive on one and poor on another; the project with the highest net present value may take seven years to pay back **[1]**. Seeing that disagreement is itself useful, because it shows the business exactly what it would be trading away, in this case liquidity in exchange for long-term value, which no single figure would reveal **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Different methods measure different things: recovery time, profitability and discounted value
> 
> AO2
> 
> - A project can rank highly on one method and poorly on another
> - Where methods disagree, the business learns what it is trading off
> - Payback addresses liquidity, which matters to a firm short of cash
> - Net present value accounts for the time value of money, which payback ignores
> - Using several reduces reliance on any one method's particular weakness
> - Different stakeholders, such as lenders and shareholders, care about different measures
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The interesting case is when the methods disagree, and that disagreement is information rather than a problem. If payback favours one project and net present value another, the business has learned what the choice actually costs it. Answers saying only that "more methods are more accurate" miss the point, because the methods are not measuring the same thing.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** qualitative factor a business should consider before making a major investment.
parts.solution_md:
Qualitative factors are influences on an investment decision that cannot be reduced to a figure in the appraisal **[1]**. One is the effect on employees: a project replacing a production line changes how people work and may make some roles redundant **[1]**. If experienced staff resist the change or leave, the business loses knowledge that took years to build and faces recruitment and training costs, so a project that appears sound on the numbers can underperform because the people expected to operate it were not brought with it **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Qualitative factors are influences that cannot be expressed as figures in the appraisal
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Employee reaction, morale and possible resistance to change
> - The effect on reputation with customers or the local community
> - Whether the project fits the business's objectives and existing strengths
> - Environmental impact and the risk of future regulation
> - The likely reaction of competitors to the investment
> - The owners' or directors' attitude to risk
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Qualitative does not mean vague. A qualitative factor still has to arrive at a consequence for the business: morale matters because turnover costs money and disrupts output, reputation matters because customers leave. Name the factor, then follow it through to something that affects performance, or the answer stays at one mark.

parts.problem_md: Explain what a positive net present value tells a business about an investment.
parts.solution_md:
A positive net present value means the discounted value of a project's future cash inflows is greater than the cost of the investment **[1]**. This tells the business the project is expected to return more than the discount rate applied to it, so it adds value rather than merely recovering its cost **[1]**. The conclusion holds only for that rate, however: if the business raised the rate to reflect more expensive borrowing, the same forecasts could produce a negative figure, so the result is a judgement about the project measured against a chosen cost of capital **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - A positive net present value means discounted inflows exceed the cost of the investment
> 
> AO2
> 
> - The project is forecast to earn more than the discount rate used, so it adds value
> - It provides a basis for accepting the project, or for ranking it against alternatives
> - The result depends on the discount rate chosen, so a higher rate could reverse it
> - It depends on forecast cash flows, which may not be achieved
> - A positive figure says nothing about the size of the investment or how long the money is committed
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always say what the figure is positive relative to. A positive net present value does not simply mean the project makes a profit; it means the project beats the discount rate the business applied. Change that rate and the same forecasts can turn negative, so naming the rate shows you understand the measure rather than just its sign.

parts.problem_md: Explain why a business discounts future cash flows when appraising an investment.
parts.solution_md:
Discounting converts cash a business expects to receive in future years into what that money is worth today **[1]**. A business does this because money received now can be put to use immediately, whether invested, used to repay borrowing or spent on another project, so a dollar in five years is genuinely worth less than a dollar today **[1]**. Without discounting, cash arriving in year five would be added to cash arriving in year one as though they were equivalent, overstating the value of long projects and possibly leading the business to choose the wrong one **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Discounting restates future cash flows in present-day values
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Money available now can be invested, so waiting carries an opportunity cost
> - Cash received sooner can repay borrowing and reduce interest
> - Forecasts further into the future are less certain, and discounting reduces their weight
> - Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money received later
> - Without discounting, projects with distant returns appear more attractive than they are
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reason is not only inflation. Even with prices completely stable, money in hand today can be invested, used to repay a loan or put into another project, so waiting has a cost of its own. Answers resting entirely on inflation give a partial reason, and the opportunity cost of waiting is the stronger half of the argument.

Net present value is the total value today of all the future cash flows expected from an investment, less the cost of making that investment **[1]**, calculated by discounting each future cash flow to what it is worth in present-day terms **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The sum of discounted future cash inflows minus the initial investment
> - The value of a project's future cash flows expressed in today's money, net of its cost
> - A measure showing whether a project adds value once the timing of cash flows is taken into account
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Present" is the word doing the work. Net present value restates future cash in today's terms before comparing it with the cost, and a definition leaving that out has described total profit instead. If your answer would read the same with no mention of time, it is not yet a definition of net present value.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** limitation of the accounting rate of return.
parts.solution_md:
The accounting rate of return compares average annual profit with the average sum invested **[1]**. Its limitation is that averaging hides when the profit arrives: two projects returning the same average each year score identically, even if one earns most of its profit in year one and the other in year five **[1]**. Money received earlier can be reinvested or used to repay borrowing, so the business would clearly prefer the first, yet the accounting rate of return gives it no way of seeing that difference **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - The accounting rate of return uses average profit against average investment
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Averaging conceals the timing of returns, so early and late profits are treated alike
> - It ignores the time value of money, unlike net present value
> - It is based on profit rather than cash, so depreciation policy affects it
> - It relies on forecasts extending across the whole life of the project
> - A percentage alone gives no indication of the size of the project
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> A limitation about timing has to put two years side by side. Writing that the accounting rate of return "ignores timing" states the fault without showing it; contrasting a project earning its profit in year one with one earning the same in year five demonstrates it. Two contrasting figures turn an assertion into an explanation.

parts.problem_md: Define the term 'accounting rate of return'.
parts.solution_md:
The accounting rate of return expresses the average annual profit from an investment as a percentage of the average amount invested **[1]**, allowing the return to be compared with a target rate or with other projects **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - Average profit divided by average investment, multiplied by 100
> - The average annual percentage return an investment is expected to generate
> - A measure allowing projects of different sizes to be compared on a common percentage basis
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both figures in this formula are averages. The syllabus gives it as average profit divided by average investment, so answers using total profit or the initial cost instead will produce a different percentage. Saying "average" twice is a quick way to show the examiner you have the right measure.

parts.problem_md: Explain **one** advantage to a business of using the payback method.
parts.solution_md:
The payback period shows how long an investment takes to recover its initial cost **[1]**. One advantage is that it suits a business whose cash is tight, because it identifies the project returning money soonest **[1]**. A firm that recovers its investment in two years rather than five has cash available again for wages, suppliers or the next project, so payback answers the question that actually constrains it, which is when the money comes back rather than how much it eventually earns **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Payback shows how quickly an investment recovers its initial cost
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Suits businesses with limited cash, since it prioritises early recovery
> - Simple to calculate and to explain to non-financial managers
> - Useful in fast-changing markets where distant forecasts are unreliable
> - Reduces risk by favouring projects with shorter exposure
> - Offers a quick way to reject unsuitable projects before detailed appraisal
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> "It is simple to calculate" is worth very little on its own, because every appraisal method is simple once it has been learned. The mark comes from saying why that simplicity matters here: a small firm with no finance department, or a market changing so fast that a five-year forecast is guesswork. Give the reason simplicity is valuable and the point develops itself.

The payback period is the length of time it takes for the cash generated by an investment to cover its initial cost **[1]**, usually expressed in years and months **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Define requires a clear statement of the meaning of the term
> 
> An example alone is not sufficient for full marks but can support a partial definition for 1 mark
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> - The time taken for cumulative net cash inflows to equal the original sum invested
> - How long a business must wait before it recovers the money it spent on a project
> - Normally measured in years and months
> 
> Accept all valid responses.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Payback measures the return of capital, not the return on it. It tells a business when its money comes back, not how much it earns, so a project can pay back quickly and still be the less profitable of two options. Keeping that distinction clear separates payback from the accounting rate of return and net present value.

parts.problem_md: Explain why a business carries out investment appraisal before committing to a major project.
parts.solution_md:
Investment appraisal is the process of assessing the likely financial returns from a project before the money is spent **[1]**. A business does this because large investments usually tie up cash for several years and cannot easily be reversed once the equipment is bought or the site is built **[1]**. Comparing the forecast returns of competing projects allows the business to put its limited finance into the option expected to generate most value, rather than discovering afterwards that a cheaper or faster-returning alternative existed **[1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explain requires a clear statement of meaning (AO1) supported by contextual development (AO2)
> 
> - Valid AO1 is awarded 1 mark
> - Valid AO2 is awarded up to 2 marks
> 
> **Indicative content**
> 
> AO1
> 
> - Investment appraisal assesses the expected financial returns of a project before money is committed
> 
> AO2
> 
> - Large investments tie up cash for years and are difficult to reverse
> - Finance is limited, so competing projects must be compared
> - It provides evidence to support a request for external funding
> - It sets a benchmark against which the project's actual performance can later be judged
> - It reduces the influence of personal preference in a major decision
> 
> Accept any other valid response.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Investment appraisal does not remove risk; it prices it. Every method works on forecast figures, so it improves the quality of the decision without guaranteeing the outcome. Answers claiming appraisal shows a project "will succeed" overstate what it does, and the more accurate point, that it makes risks visible and comparable, is the one that earns marks.
